Title: Tourney thoughts - time for a change?

Messages.Author: legbiter
Messages.Body:
The Casual/Competitive thread plus some of the other recent-ish musings
about ratings, the metagame and so on have got me thinking about whether
the tourney scene and the game generally might benefit from a bit of a
shake-up. In particular, i wonder whether there is a case for a
different kind of tournament in which people may bring and play up to
THREE decks rather than one [qualifiers would have to pick one of them
for the final]. You would have to make people provide lists of all three
decks and the judge would probably have to do quite a bit of checking
[both of which are bad things]; plus, it would become harder for people
with limited card pools to compete [also a bad thing]. On the plus side,
you would get far more variety and i suspect more interesting games and
finals. i'm aware that this is not a completely new idea and i'ld value
the opinions/experience of the newsgroup about this [which is why i'm
posting]; and i'ld also like to know whether people in the UK/North
Europe might be interested in a pilot of this idea, a non-sanctioned
tournament to be held in Portsmouth [or another English location, if
someone else wants to volunteer to host it], perhaps sometime this
summer. Thanks in advance for your thoughts!

--

I don't think so. The reason Sten is "ducking" is because this idea has
been brought up before. Sideboards don't work well in Jyhad because you
only play one game against any given set of opponents. In Magic, sideboards
are used in tournaments where you're matched up against the same person for
more than one game - and then, you're supposed to return to your original,
non-sideboarded deck before playing the first game of the next match.
You're not supposed to be out scouting future opponents in other games to
determine which sideboard cards you should use.

We can use these same sideboard rules. And, since you only play one game
in a Jyhad "match", you can never use it. So why bother?

Fred

The problem with this approach, though, is that if you
take out all the current top-of-the-power-curve cards,
you'll just replace them with the not-quite-top-of-the-
power-curve cards. I mean, for some things (Hostile
Takeover, Temptation of Greater Power, Temptation, Form
of Corruption, Parity Shift) there's no substitute, but
if you ditch Majesty and Catatonic Fear, Staredown is
waiting right behind; similarly for Undead Strength vs,
say, Mighty Grapple. And if you rule out *all* the good
cards, what are people going to play with? Just the
crappy ones? What's going to make that more fun, just
the fact that until now people haven't been playing with
cards with those titles and pictures?

It seems to me that if you want people to be "more creative"
in their deckbuilding and choices, you just need to encourage
them to be more creative somehow. I don't know why they
aren't self-motivated to do what's not expected (I've been
playing lots of attempts at Salubri Spirit Marionette and
Agaitas vamp-stealing lately), but I think if your players
were to venture outside these twelve decks and few dozen
cards that you mention, they'd find that an awful lot of the
cards for VTES are quite competitively playable. Sure, there
are only so many different basic methods for killing people,
but there are a lot of ways to go about it.

And if you're tired of seeing the basic methods for killing
people in the first place, maybe you're just a little burned
out on VTES and should take a break until it seems like fun
again...

Or play draft. Draft is (a) lots of fun and (b) doesn't
have most of the 'power cards' influencing it very much.
Especially if you do Sabbat War draft, where 5th Tradition,
Blood Doll, and Minion Tap don't even exist...

> It shouldn't be
> the case that certain cards determine the clans being played rather than

Well, you know, most of the 'abusive' stuff you mention can
be counteracted by playing enough countermeasures in the
deck you want to surprise people with. Loads of Suddens,
for example, make you pretty ToGP/Hostile-proof. Likewise
loads of Delaying Tactics make you Parity Shift-proof.
That's not to say that you should have to play with these
specific methods in order to compete, but if you feel like
shutting down the decks whose predictability is bugging you,
well, it's easy enough to do... :-)

Josh

make it feasible to keep all the other players under your

easily pushed - might give everyone more time to develop
a stable position. But it wouldn't exactly be VTES as
we know it.

would be a *really* dumb possibility). Sideboarding in VTES, by virtue of the

You can do this in non competetive games all you want already.

I haven't read the entire thread here, but thought people might be
interested in a tidbid about sideboards (and I get to tell a story!).

About 4-5 years ago, I attended the annual U-Con event in Ann Arbor, Mi.
where Richard Garfield was actually running some Magic:TG events.
I'd signed up to play in an unconventional sealed/draft format that he
was running later that afternoon, and with plenty of time (hours) before

Things from OuterSpace (Boardgame).

Anyhow, Richard Garfield arrives in the room early and sees us playing
one of his favorite games :-) Seeing as he's all chatty, I decided to
ask him a question about Magic:TG that had been bothering me since
the Tournament scene formed.

I basically asked "Why did Magic:TG develop sideboarding?", having
been one of those players that got in just post-beta I never quite
understood why sideboarding should be included into the game.

* His response was practically as simple as my question.
Per Mr. Garfield (I paraphrase) "Sideboarding was created to encourage
people to play decks that included more than one color".
So the inclusion of sideboarding was to encourage more than one
dimensional play.

[*See, I actually got somewhere with this story :-)]

VTES doesn't have that problem, or at least not on the same scale as
Magic:TG did. Much like Peter, I don't believe that Sideboarding is
feasible or necessary in VTES.

The only mechanic I attempted to bring into Vampire from the Magic
circuit was a Mulligan variant. (listed post-message for your perusal).
It seemed to work okay (we tried it out in my group awhile back), but
we tend to play the "real" game and steer away from house rules.

Okay, I'm out the door. Happy holidays everyone!

Bernie Bresnahan
Lansing, Mi.

======================================================

VTES Mulligan:

- A player may opt to draw a new hand and crypt before play begins.
- Each player that does so will place their current hand back into their
library
- Re-shuffle the library and draw seven new cards
- That player will also place the Vampires in their uncontrolled region
back into their Crypt
- After shuffling Crypt cards, they draw and place Three Vampires (only)
in their uncontrolled region
- A player may only Mulligan once per game

Messages.Author: jspektr
Messages.Body:
Are people honestly articulating the real problem here?

As I see it, the complaint is that if you have a clever idea for a
focused deck, and you sit down next to the wrong predator or prey, you
are screwed.

I think that is a benefit, not a problem.

Sure, I've played my share of focused decks. But when playing a
serious game, I always try to make sure my decks have a strategy
flexible enough to get around an opponent that spoils them. We have a
weekly Jyhad group, and when we sit down for a tournament-level game,
I always look forward to sitting down next to a deck that ruins my
strategy. That's what can happen in a tournament, and your deck should
be flexible enough to handle it.

This is the inherent defense against mono-discipline decks, if they
are too focused they will be vulnerable to bad seating. This is a good
thing, and should serve to discourage super-focused decks. And it
should encourage people to include a few cards they normally wouldn't.
After I played an Anson/Parthenon Temptation of Greater Power/Golconda
deck one week, everyone started keeping a couple of Sudden Reversals
in their decks, which is good, because it discourages fragile,
overly-focused deck designs. After a spate of weenie-bleed decks, a
few Atonements made their way into most decks, and anyone with votes
packs a few Anarchist Uprisings. These are all cards that are normally
good regardless of the situation, and become even better if someone is
playing a particular focused deck that can sweep a table if there are
no checks on it.

JSpektr
